results.title: The Ghana cedi has recorded four consecutive trading days of appreciation, closing at GH¢11.65 to the US dollar on Thursday, 15 October 2026.
results.description:
The Ghana cedi has recorded four consecutive trading days of appreciation, closing at GH¢11.65 to the US dollar on Thursday, 15 October 2026. This represents a 1.5% gain since 7 October 2026.

The recovery reflects improved dollar liquidity in the foreign exchange market, supported by the Ghana Gold Board's direct supply of foreign exchange to commercial banks.

A stronger cedi helps reduce the cost of imports, including petroleum products, and provides relief to businesses and consumers at a time of rising pressure on fuel prices.

The GoldBod remains committed to sustaining foreign exchange supply to the market in support of currency stability and Ghana's broader economic resilience.

#GoldBod #GhanaGold

results.title: Two quiet but important shifts in how Ghana is financing itself.
results.description:
Two quiet but important shifts in how Ghana is financing itself. COCOBOD is raising money locally on the stock exchange to buy cocoa this season instead of leaning as heavily on external loans. At the same time, GoldBod has been selling hundreds of millions of dollars from gold operations into the banking system, giving banks more foreign exchange and offering the cedi some breathing room.
Neither of these is magic. Farmers still need to be paid properly, and businesses still need dollars at reasonable rates. But they are examples of trying to manage with more of our own resources. The question for ordinary people is whether the stability reaches the market, the farmgate and the shop shelf.
#SocietyAndDiplomacy

results.title: His government is sleepwalking into a serious economic crisis.
results.description:
His government is sleepwalking into a serious economic crisis. The fundamental mistake was abandoning the GH¢16-to-the-dollar exchange rate he inherited and pursuing a currency policy that appears increasingly costly to sustain. He is now reportedly committing roughly $1.2 billion a month in gold-related foreign exchange interventions to keep the cedi around GH¢11 to the dollar, while the economy struggles to create jobs for an estimated 500,000 people entering the labour market every year.

What is the point of defending the cedi at such a high cost if the economy is not generating enough productive jobs, expanding exports, and building sustainable sources of foreign exchange? A stronger currency means little if it rests on costly interventions rather than stronger fundamentals.

This is precisely the kind of economic strategy that demands urgent scrutiny. The government must explain the true cost of these interventions, their sustainability, and the measurable benefits they deliver to ordinary Ghanaians. What is even more troubling is the apparent absence of an urgent push from those closest to the president for a fundamental policy reassessment. Ghana cannot afford to confuse short-term currency stability with genuine economic recovery. The country needs a credible course correction before the costs become even harder to reverse.
